b:
v:Though ages pass,
though epics fade,
she is the angel of imagination
who never fades from my dreams.
She is not only an angel;
she is both
mother
and wife.
In her world
both of these
have a new meaning.
This
is her story
h:A Smile

It was a well-known school. The crowd for first-year admissions was surging. That was when I saw Saradha there. Wheat-brown skin. Hair oiled and combed back. Two earrings you could only see if you looked closely. A cotton sari that covered exactly what needed covering. One of her hands held another angel tightly.
I am the school clerk. If you want it in Tamil, the "writing officer". But there is not much to write there. The computer changed my job long ago.

Saradha, who came next, slowly pushed the admission form through the hole in the glass. At the top, a Pillaiyar suzhi. How villagey, I thought to myself. The child's name was Venmathi. She really was a "white moon". She must take after her father.

It said the husband was abroad. The respectable word "business" filled the blank for occupation. I checked everything, entered it into the computer, and gestured for them to go in. She went in with half a smile. Venmathi waved with her free hand, the other gripped tight by her mother.

In the evening, after work, I came home, washed my hands and feet, and peeped at the house opposite. Saradha had not come home yet. Yes! It has been a month since Saradha moved into the flat opposite mine. The half smile she gave when she arrived has continued to this day.
Venmathi is six. A darling child who sticks to everyone the moment she sees them. Who could help enjoying that restless, fidgety childishness?

The Saradha I saw today is the Saradha I see every day in the flat opposite. I only learned her name was Saradha when the apartment secretary called her. Though she had been here a month, we had never spoken. When Venmathi played downstairs, she would claim me as "Uncle". Saradha never took any notice of it. Nor did she stop it

To me Saradha was a puzzle. The eagerness you feel reading a mystery story came over me whenever I saw her. It wasn't lust. Nor was it love. A feeling that can't be held in words. Certainly neither of the two I just named.
While I was eating the dinner I had cooked, a shuffle of slippers. The two pairs of slippers told me it was Saradha. My heart said, open it and look. I flung the door open.

Hearing the sudden noise, Saradha turned round. For a moment her face showed she hadn't expected it, but she pulled herself together. At once she turned away like a stone without feeling and slid the key into the keyhole
I hadn't expected much, but something had prodded my manhood. Still, the sleepy, silent language Venmathi spoke beside her soothed me
As I gave up and turned to go back inside, Saradha's voice: "Excuse me"!
The first word she had let fall in the month since she first saw me. A feeling inside. No butterflies flew in my stomach.
I turned round as if I'd been waiting for it.
"Today............ morning........................ school ................." The words came with hesitation

I understood that hesitation, the hesitation of speaking to a new stranger out of necessity. Not wanting to make her more uncomfortable, I said, "Venmathi's admission is being processed. I'll let you know if there's any further development"
"Thank you," said Saradha, short as a gem.
As I began to say, "Nice to meet you. I am .........", Saradha went into her flat with a full smile. Only Venmathi's lollipop stick was left outside
h:A Gift

Friday. I decided to go to the temple before going to school. There was an Amman temple near the house. Since it was Friday, the temple would be crowded with women. That might also have been a reason I went to the temple. I don't know.

As I came out after walking round the inner courtyard, Saradha appeared in front of me. The red sari suited her well. Her face showed more happiness than usual. That too somehow made her look more beautiful.
Saradha smiled at me. Venmathi was with her. When she said "Uncle" in her baby talk, for a moment it seemed I didn't need to come to the temple to see God.
Smiling back at Saradha out of duty, I stroked Venmathi's head and came out. I made up my mind to come to the temple next Friday too.

There was a lot of work at school today. The list of children selected for first year had come. Letters had to be written to the selected homes. Venmathi was one of them. I must go and tell Saradha today
I thought of going to Saradha as soon as I got home. I was sweaty. I'll have a bath and then go, I decided
After my bath I put on the best clothes I had. I must give Venmathi something. I took a chocolate from the fridge and came out

None of the flats in our apartment block had a calling bell. So you had to knock on the door. I knocked three times, hesitantly. It would have been a wonder if Saradha heard it. I heard the bolt being drawn inside. I stood ready

Saradha didn't come, as I'd expected. It was Venmathi who opened the door. You could see at once that the door handle was out of her reach. The beauty of her standing on tiptoe holding the door handle: I have no simile for it
Before I could ask whether her mother was in, Saradha came. Seeing her mother, Venmathi flew off like a sparrow and sat down in front of the TV.
Saradha had a ladle in one hand. She must have been cooking.
I thought she would look at me as if to say "Why have you come!" But instead she invited me to come in and sit. As I sat on a chair she gestured and went to turn off the stove.

That was the first time I saw Saradha's home. It was more beautiful than mine. The whole flat was full of photos of Venmathi. I understood that she was Saradha's world. But I couldn't find a single picture of Venmathi's father anywhere

Saradha came and sat opposite me. The way she sat on the edge of the seat reminded me that I was an outsider, a stranger. "What is it?" she asked. When I told her Venmathi had got admission, the joy showed clearly on her face. She called Venmathi and told her to say "thank you". I accepted that meaningless word for their sake

I held out my chocolate, saying it was a small gift for Venmathi. Instead of taking it, Venmathi stood there staring at Saradha. I thought she must be the first child ever to stand like that on seeing a chocolate.
"She has lactose intolerance," Saradha said, worried. I didn't understand what it was. But I didn't want to show my ignorance in front of her. I must look up what it was as soon as I got home.

"Oh! Sorry," I said. Still, I felt I must give Venmathi something. I opened my wallet. There was a picture of Pillaiyarpatti Ganapathi. I took it out, held it out, and blessed her to study well. Saradha laughed. I remembered how I had laughed to myself that day at the Pillaiyar suzhi on the admission form. I felt ashamed
As I said goodbye and came out, Saradha came out too. "Once again, thank you," she said, and I said "welcome" and went to my flat. A little while after I shut my door, I heard Saradha's door close.
h:Farewell
Days passed, and many months too. Meanwhile my acquaintance with Saradha had become a friendship. Certainly it was the friendship of neighbours. Neither of us crossed its borders and limits.
Venmathi stuck to me, calling "Uncle, Uncle". In all that time Saradha didn't seem to have learned my name. To her too I had become Venmathi's uncle.

One day Saradha asked, "Could you take Venmathi to school and bring her back?" I agreed. There was some joy in having become someone she trusted. Meanwhile Saradha had started going to some job. I didn't know what job. I never asked. By the time I brought Venmathi back, she would be home too.
That day I brought Venmathi home as usual. Saradha seemed to have come back already. Someone had come to the house too. There were slippers outside.
When I knocked, Saradha came out. Saradha's usual smile wasn't there. Somehow she looked troubled.
"Sorry, could you keep Venmathi at your place for a little while?" she asked. It was neither pleading nor an order. Her decision that I would understand her awkward situation was clear.
I had no reason at all to refuse.

I agreed and took Venmathi to my flat. There was food at home. I put food on a plate for Venmathi and she started eating. I wasn't hungry; more than eating, my heart was eager to know what was troubling Saradha
About two hours later Saradha knocked on my door. The door was open. I asked her to come in.
She had been crying. It showed in her eyes. I didn't want to see Saradha like that.
She said "Thank you" and got ready to take Venmathi away.

Some feeling told me to call her. The strangeness between us had lessened and a friendship had grown. But I didn't know whether it was the kind of friendship that could interfere in someone's private life. Since Saradha came here, no one, relative or stranger, had come looking for her. As far as I knew, she hadn't grown close to anyone in this apartment block. So my heart told me I had the right to stand by her. I didn't know whether that right was more than I was due. But I wanted to take it.
"Saradha, is everything alright?"
I had never called her by her name before. It must have startled her, but she must also have expected me to ask something. I understood that when I looked at her
She told Venmathi to go home and came and sat opposite me. The distance between us showed the gap in our acquaintance. She said nothing. She sat quietly. She didn't know where to begin
I thought I might as well begin
"Who was that who came to your place?"
I felt as if I were trying to cross the border wall of a country no one may enter. She, though, was somehow relieved that I had begun
"My mother." There was bitterness in the answer
After a while: "You wouldn't have seen Venmathi's father?"
"Yes, he does business abroad, doesn't he?"
"He and I have been separated for four years"
Soon after Saradha came, I had understood that she wasn't living with her husband. I had even thought there might have been a divorce
"Now Venmathi's father expects Venmathi to be with him"
I didn't know what to say. The dried tracks of the tears that had run from Saradha's eyes showed clearly. I kept looking at them.
Saradha had no need to tell me all this. But she wasn't telling me because she wanted me to hear it. She was making some decision. The strain of it showed on her face.
h:Auspicious

Saradha's story was nothing new. It was the usual Tamil cinema story: young love. A marriage without the parents' blessing. Life abroad with the husband. As love and desire faded, suspicion that clung to the husband and new company. That's all there was to Saradha's past. She had put up with it patiently too. When even Venmathi's birth didn't solve her problems, she came here with her daughter.

Venmathi's birth had brought the two families together. It didn't answer her confusion. After some time, her husband came to apologise and take them back. But her self-respect wouldn't give way to that. She refused. From then on she was a "single mother"
"Why is he suddenly asking for Venmathi now?"
"He expects that if he calls Venmathi, I'll come too. He's even sending my own mother as his messenger for that."
"Then your family wants you to go back to him. Right?"
"Yes. Amma, Appa. That's what they'd think, isn't it?"
"Then are you going to go with him?" I hid the disappointment I felt.
She laughed. There was scorn in it. I didn't understand why

"I decided when I left him. That was the full stop to my life with him. I have no wish to turn it into a comma now and carry on. Venmathi is everything to me. But I have a life of my own too, self-respect, all of it. I'm not ready to give that up"
"Then are you going to live alone with Venmathi?"
A silence surrounded us. She broke at that question. For a moment the words wouldn't come.
"No...... I'm going to send Venmathi to her father….”
She held back her tears. I should say something comforting. But in my heart there were a thousand questions. I could ask only one.
"Why?"

"I haven't studied much. So I couldn't get a good job either. I definitely can't raise Venmathi on my own. And I'm not ready for another marriage for that. He may have been a bad husband, but he is a good father. Only he can give Venmathi a good future. This is for her best"

In these times, can you hand a girl child over to a man alone? Can a man raise a girl child alone? Can Saradha live apart from Venmathi? What if tomorrow Venmathi forgets Saradha? Will this society accept all this? I felt like asking all of it. But I didn't. Saradha would have thought about all of it, and she would have some answer to it all. The firmness in her eyes told me that the decision she had made was final.
Venmathi came running from somewhere and whispered something sweet in Saradha's ear, and Saradha took her leave of me.

After that, many things happened over many days. Days went by with many people coming to Saradha's flat and Saradha shouting at them many times. But one thing was clear to me. My days with Venmathi were numbered. That was certain.
Venmathi knew nothing of what was happening. Often, when she came to play at my flat, she would ask, "Why is Amma crying?" I would manage with some lie that suited her.

At last the day came for Venmathi to go to her father. Venmathi's paternal grandparents had come to take her. Saradha was brave. She didn't cry. To Venmathi it was a holiday trip. She didn't know she was leaving her mother for good. I took out the lactose-free chocolate I had not forgotten to buy and held it out. I wasn't there when Venmathi left. I had gone to school
When I came back, only one pair of slippers was left outside Saradha's flat. After that the flat stayed locked for many days.
It has been three months since Venmathi went abroad. Saradha has found some job in some country. Today she is vacating her flat.

In this time Saradha has recovered a great deal. But this society has not. There was indeed the crowd that asked behind her back, "Call that a mother!", and the few "pure" hearts that cast their hooks at her. Saradha paid them no attention

As far as I was concerned, there was honesty in Saradha's eyes. There was clarity. That was enough for me. Saradha was no revolutionary woman, nor a heroine from the epics. This is no film, where a woman living alone is given a job and lifted up. This is reality. Culture and religion have locked this society up. But not everyone can live inside those bounds. They choose, willingly or unwillingly. This world is not yet mature enough to understand that. That is the truth

The time came for Saradha to leave. Before going, she knocked on my door to say goodbye. When I opened it she said, "Thank you………for everything." I said, "Have a safe journey!" and as I turned to go in,
"Excuse me, sorry, you never told me your name. If you don't mind, what is your name?"
Holding out the lollipop stick in my hand to her, I said,
"Train friend"
note: A Pillaiyar suzhi is the small curl, a symbol of Ganesha, that many Tamils write at the top of a page for luck. Venmathi means "white moon". Pillaiyarpatti is a famous Ganesha temple in Tamil Nadu. A "train friend" (rayil snēkitan) is someone you grow close to on a journey and part from at the station, never to meet again.
